chunk_findings.detail: `_param_end` still treats the first `}` as the end of `${...}` and never skips a quoted span, so a `)` that bash still considers part of the expansion is taken as the `$()` closer and the rest of the substitution is dropped. For `echo "$(echo ${x:-"}")}; git push origin main)"`, bash’s matching `}` is the one after the quoted `}`, the `)` before that `}` is literal text inside `${x:-...}`, and bash then runs `git push origin main` inside the substitution. `_param_end` returns at the `}` inside the quotes; `_find_body` then stops at that `)`, the body appended is only `echo ${x:-"}`, and `_dquote_end` leaves `git push` as ordinary double-quoted text, so `check` returns None. The later hunk that touches `_param_end` is not this function: the body shown here still has no quote walk.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_param_end

chunk_findings.detail: `_has_esac` still searches the raw string for a bare `esac` and ignores quotes, so a `case` word plus an `esac` that is only literal text makes `_skip_span` enter case mode and swallow the real `$()` closer. For `echo "$(echo case x); git push origin main; esac"`, bash closes the substitution at the `)` after `x` and prints the rest, including `git push`, without executing it. `_has_esac` still sees the quoted `esac`, `_case_end` walks past that `)`, and the body appended to `bodies` includes `git push origin main`, so the guard refuses a command bash never runs.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_has_esac

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten descent still treats `-c` as a whole word: `"-c" in head` is false and `head.index("-c")` never runs for a clustered flag. Given `bash -exc 'git push origin main'` (and `sh -xc 'git push origin main'`), bash enables `-e -x -c` and executes `git push origin main`, but the words are `['bash', '-exc', 'git push origin main']`, so the payload is never `_split` and `check` returns None. The same holds for `-exc` on the other shells in `_SHELLS`. This is the prior clustered-flag miss; this hunk does not call a flag splitter.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_commands

chunk_findings.detail: The new hunks only change `${...}` scanning, unclosed-sub mask clamping, and `_sh_c`. They do not make `esac` quote-aware, so the earlier case still fails: given `echo "$(echo case x); git push origin main; esac"`, bash closes the substitution at the `)` after `x` and does not run `git push`, but a raw `esac` search still throws case mode past that `)`, the substitution body is kept, and `check` refuses a command bash never executes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_has_esac

chunk_findings.detail: `_sh_c` treats any short token containing `c` as the shell’s `-c` and does not stop at the first operand. Given `bash ./tool.sh -cache 'git push origin main'`, bash runs `./tool.sh` with those two arguments and does not execute `git push`; the old exact `"-c" in head` check left this alone, but `"c" in "cache"` now returns that index and `_split`s the next word, so `check` refuses a command that never runs. The same misfire hits `bash -ocpipefail 'git push origin main'`, where `-o` consumes `cpipefail` and the quoted string is the script name, not a `-c` payload.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_sh_c

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier probe does not refute this: `_has_esac` still does a raw `find("esac")` plus `_bare_word`, with no quote or `$(...)` depth, and `_skip_span` enters case mode on that result. For `echo "$(echo case x); git push origin main; esac"`, bash closes `$(` at the `)` after `x` and prints `; git push origin main; esac` as literal text inside the double quotes, so `git push` never runs. The guard does the opposite: from inside that `$(`, `_has_esac` sees the later bare `esac` (the `"` after it is not alphanumeric), `_case_end` swallows the real `)` closer, `_find_body` returns the end of the string, and `bodies` includes `git push`, so `check` refuses a command bash does not execute.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_has_esac

chunk_findings.detail: `_sh_c` treats `o`/`O` as consuming the next argv word only when the whole token is exactly `-o`/`-O`. If that letter is the last character of a cluster, the inner loop `break`s and the outer loop only does `i += 1`, so the optname is mistaken for the script operand and parsing stops. Given `bash -xo pipefail -c 'git push origin main'` (same for `bash -xO extglob -c 'git push origin main'`), bash enables `-x`, applies `-o`/`-O` to the next word, then runs the `-c` payload; `_sh_c` returns -1 and `check` does not refuse `git push`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_sh_c

chunk_findings.detail: A long option is skipped as a single word (`i += 1`) and never consumes an argument, so the following operand is treated as the script name and `-c` after it is ignored. This is a regression from the old `"-c" in body` scan. Given `bash --rcfile /tmp/rc -c 'git push origin main'` (same for `bash --init-file /tmp/rc -c 'git push origin main'`), bash still takes the `-c` string and runs `git push`; `_sh_c` returns -1 at `/tmp/rc` and `check` returns None.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_sh_c

evidence.budget_forced: re-review _sh_c -o/-O-cluster and --rcfile fix that answers confirmed #2 #3

chunk_findings.detail: `_has_esac` treats any later bare `esac` in the whole buffer as closing a case statement, and `_skip_span` then jumps to it while scanning a `)`-closed body. `$((` is classified as arithmetic and `_sub_body` records no body for that span, but `_scan` still drops from the `$` through the jumped-to `esac`. Given `echo $((case 0)); git push origin main; echo esac`, bash rejects the arithmetic word, then still runs `git push` (`echo $((case 0)); echo AFTER; echo esac` prints `AFTER`), while the guard drops `git push` from the line and never puts it in `bodies`, so `check` allows it. The earlier probe only shows `check` returns None for a quoted `esac` bash does not execute; it does not exercise this path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_sub_body

chunk_findings.detail: `_sh_c` treats any token that does not start with `-` as the script operand and returns -1, so a leading `+` option hides a later `-c`. Bash accepts the `set` `+` forms on invocation (`+x`, `+o`, `+O`). Given `bash +x -c 'git push origin main'` (same for `bash +o pipefail -c 'git push origin main'`), bash still parses options and runs the `-c` payload; `_sh_c` returns -1 at `+x`/`+o` and `check` allows the push.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_sh_c

chunk_findings.detail: Returning at the first `c` in a cluster ignores an `o`/`O` that follows `c` and consumes the next argv word. Given `bash -co pipefail 'git push origin main'` (same for `bash -cO extglob 'git push origin main'` and `bash -xco pipefail 'git push origin main'`), bash sets the `-o`/`-O` name from `pipefail`/`extglob` and runs the following `-c` string; `_sh_c` returns the index of `-co` and the payload inspected is `pipefail`, so `git push` is never seen and `check` returns None.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_sh_c
